l: Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: This document is the EMNLP 2024 paper “Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation,” by Qinyuan Cheng, Xiaonan Li, Shimin Li, Qin Zhu, Zhangyue Yin, Yunfan Shao, Linyang Li, Tianxiang Sun, Hang Yan, and Xipeng Qiu, affiliated with Fudan University, Shanghai AI Laboratory, and Shanghai Collaborative Innovation Center of Intelligent Visual Computing. It addresses when Retrieval-Augmented Generation should retrieve external documents rather than relying on a large language model alone. Retrieval can improve factual reliability, but unnecessary or poor-quality retrieval may increase cost, interfere with responses, or harm creativity. The paper introduces Unified Active Retrieval (UAR), a plug-and-play framework that freezes the underlying large language model and uses lightweight single-layer MLP classifiers over its final input-token hidden state. UAR makes retrieval decisions through four orthogonal criteria: retrieval intent, knowledge intensity, time sensitivity, and model familiarity or self-awareness. Its Unified Active Retrieval Criteria (UAR-Criteria) organizes these judgments in a prioritized decision tree. If retrieval is needed, retrieved documents are appended to the instruction; otherwise, the original generation format is preserved. After reviewing prior active retrieval, temporal reasoning, mutable-fact, and self-awareness work, the paper evaluates UAR on the new Active Retrieval Benchmark (AR-Bench) and six downstream datasets with 7B and 13B Llama2 models. UAR exceeds FLARE, Self-RAG, and SKR in retrieval-timing accuracy across intent-aware, knowledge-aware, time-aware, and self-aware cases. It also achieves the strongest overall downstream results while retrieving selectively, notably for time-sensitive TAQA and FreshQA questions and unfamiliar TriviaQA and WebQuestions facts. Further analysis finds self-aware retrieval decisions most difficult. Fine-tuning the whole model yields only slight self-awareness gains over value-head classification while increasing latency and parameter requirements. Results also vary with the number of reference documents and with retrieval frequency. The paper concludes that multifaceted, low-cost retrieval timing can avoid needless or harmful augmentation while preserving model capabilities. Limitations include a focus on short-text, mainly knowledge-question-answering settings; only one retrieval call; potentially incomplete criteria; and an unexplored deeper classifier design. The work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and Fudan University’s CFFF platform.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation, Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval Augmented Generation is an approach to address LLM hallucination that retrieves relevant documents before generation and appends retrieved external information to the original user input through a RAG template. It aims to improve factual correctness, especially for questions requiring current or missing information, while directing the model to use only passages relevant to the question. Its central issue is that retrieval is not always beneficial: applying it to every instruction can add irrelevant or incorrect knowledge, increase latency, and impair creativity and versatility. Thus, always-retrieval uses it for every generation and never-retrieval for none, while UAR introduces selective retrieval to preserve internal capabilities and supply information when needed.

l: Active Retrieval, Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Active Retrieval is the determination of whether and when external information should be retrieved for a particular instruction in RAG, rather than retrieving for every instruction or never using retrieval augmentation. It is crucial to RAG because selective retrieval can preserve model versatility, reduce retrievals, and avoid interference from low-quality results. Earlier methods use knowledge-aware criteria based on factual relevance or self-aware criteria based on LLM self-awareness, but they commonly rely on one criterion, specialized procedures, and a single scenario, increasing latency and failing in complex real-world situations. UAR broadens the decision to multiple criteria: user intent, factual knowledge requirements, time sensitivity, and internal knowledge. Its results and evaluation across scenarios support multifaceted decisions and improved retrieval-timing judgments.

l: Unified Active Retrieval, Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Unified Active Retrieval (UAR) is a unified, plug-and-play active retrieval framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation that decides whether retrieval is needed for diverse user instructions. It addresses two challenges in active retrieval by turning four orthogonal retrieval-timing criteria into classification tasks: user intent, knowledge awareness, time awareness, and self awareness. For each criterion or scenario, UAR trains a lightweight binary classifier, described as a single-layer MLP or value head, on the last-layer hidden states of a fixed LLM. The LLM remains frozen and its parameters are not changed. The classifiers determine whether to retrieve; when retrieval is activated, retrieved information is appended to the original instruction, while unnecessary retrieval is avoided. Its central result is multifaceted, comprehensive retrieval-timing judgment with negligible or minimal extra inference cost and no loss of model capabilities. UAR reports the highest overall active retrieval accuracy on the Active Retrieval Benchmark for 7B and 13B models, downstream overall scores of 50.49 and 53.26 respectively, and better results than existing work, including FLARE across all AR-Bench scenarios. Its criterion accuracies are 91.88 for intent-aware, 90.38 for knowledge-aware, 86.69 for time-aware, and 72.32 for self-aware retrieval. However, UAR has lower accuracy than the corresponding single classifiers in all evaluated scenarios, with self awareness a bottleneck. Across downstream tasks, UAR avoids much unnecessary retrieval on DROP and GSM8K, retrieves almost perfectly for time-sensitive TAQA questions, and selectively retrieves for TriviaQA and WebQuestions. It outperforms always-retrieval and never-retrieval on WebQuestions; on TriviaQA, it performs best with fewer reference documents, can match always-retrieval with more documents, and requires fewer retrieval calls.

l: UAR-Criteria, Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: UAR-Criteria is a unified active retrieval decision procedure and multifaceted decision tree for processing diverse retrieval scenarios uniformly. Its central feature is a priority-ordered sequence of criteria: it first checks intent-aware retrieval intent; absent explicit intent, it checks knowledge intensity, then time sensitivity, then whether the model knows the relevant information. It activates retrieval for explicitly retrieval-oriented instructions, time-sensitive knowledge-intensive tasks, or unfamiliar knowledge-intensive tasks, and cancels retrieval for non-knowledge-intensive or model-known instructions.

s: Retrieval supplies external information for factual, time-sensitive, or explicitly retrieval-oriented instructions, but is not always helpful: irrelevant results can hinder internal knowledge and add latency through retrieval and longer input. UAR decides whether to trigger it, retrieving for explicit intent, time-sensitive needs, or unknown knowledge; documents are appended to the instruction, otherwise it remains unchanged. By reducing and selecting retrieval calls, UAR improves over never-retrieval on WebQuestions and matches similar TriviaQA performance with fewer calls than always-retrieval.

s: Large language models are language models, commonly based on decoder-only architecture, that have developed rapidly in coding, writing, and reasoning but can generate fabricated or non-factual information. They can be trained to assess whether they know answers and express this capability. UAR uses that assessment to decide when external retrieval is needed, while keeping model parameters fixed during classifier training.

Reported experiments show that UAR significantly outperforms existing methods.

l: RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This is a paper in the Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, titled “RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation,” by Kiseung Kim and Jay-Yoon Lee of the Graduate School of Data Science at Seoul National University. It addresses a weakness of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for open-domain question answering: retrieved contexts may be irrelevant and distract a generator, reducing answer accuracy. Traditional RAG weights contexts using retriever relevance scores, while approaches such as RALM use concatenated contexts for large-language-model in-context learning. The authors propose RE-RAG, which adds a detachable relevance estimator (RE) to retrieval and generation. The RE estimates both contexts’ relative usefulness for answering a question and confidence in the retrieved context set. It is weakly supervised from question-answer data without labels identifying correct contexts. RE-RAG reranks retrieved contexts, replaces retriever similarity weights with normalized RE scores, and jointly trains generator, relevance-estimation, and token losses. It can be trained with a small language model and then used with larger language models. Experiments on Natural Questions and TriviaQA compare RE-RAG with traditional RAG, FiD, FiD-KD, MonoT5, and large language model approaches. RE-RAG evaluates 100 retrieved contexts and uses the top 25 at inference. Reported results show that it generally improves over comparable baselines, outperforms traditional RAG with the same total parameter count, competes with FiD-based models, and improves reranking and unanswerable-set classification. Applied to Llama2, RE surpasses Self-RAG, though TriviaQA results depend more on the generator. RE also generalizes better than FiD-KD on unseen datasets, and ablations indicate benefits from reranking, relevance scoring, normalization, and generator-informed loss. The paper further uses RE confidence for decoding: low-confidence sets can be classified as unanswerable, or the system can selectively favor an LLM’s parametric knowledge. This mixed strategy generally improves TriviaQA while preserving Natural Questions performance. The authors conclude that RE-RAG strengthens RAG and can augment modern large language models. They note that the work focuses on single-hop QA; multi-hop effectiveness remains unverified, and future work should assess whether parametric knowledge can answer a query before deeming it unanswerable. The research received support from the National Research Foundation of Korea, Seoul National University, and computing-resource contributors.

s: This work is titled “RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation.” It concerns improving open-domain QA performance and interpretability with a relevance estimator in retrieval-augmented generation.

l: RE-RAG, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RE-RAG is a proposed framework, model, and RAG system for open-domain question answering that extends traditional retrieval-augmented generation with an external relevance estimator (RE). Its central feature is the RE module: it evaluates question-context relevance and confidence, reranks initially retrieved contexts, and supplies more precise relevance scores for answer generation. RE-RAG replaces similarity-based marginalization weights with normalized RE scores and jointly trains its components. The estimator’s information is used in question answering and decoding, supporting the handling of unanswerable or low-confidence context sets while improving interpretability. At inference, the system uses an extra context-evaluation module and 25 contexts. It was evaluated on Natural Questions and TriviaQA, where reported results generally outperform comparable FiD-KD and other baselines; RE-RAGFlan-large reached 62.5 F1 on Natural Questions and 78.7 F1 on TriviaQA among the small-generator group. With the same total parameter count, it achieves higher accuracy than traditional RAG and performs competitively with FiD-based models. Ablations indicate that both improved context selection through reranking and improved context weighting through relevance scores contribute to performance. The framework is reported to enhance traditional RAG, but its effectiveness has not yet been sufficiently evaluated on multi-hop QA tasks; extending it to such tasks is future work.

l: open-domain QA, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Open-domain QA is evaluated on Natural Questions and TriviaQA, mainly by exact match, with F1 and accuracy also reported. It has studied extracting and using answers from retrieved documents, while generative models such as T5 and BART have become increasingly common. RE-RAG aims to improve its performance and interpretability.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a framework and traditional QA system that combines parametric knowledge with external, nonparametric knowledge for open-domain question answering and knowledge-intensive natural language generation. It uses a retriever to obtain query-related contexts and a generator to produce answers for question-context pairs, then aggregates or marginalizes answers across multiple contexts using document relevance or retrieval-based similarity scores. RAG has shown promising progress and state-of-the-art performance, and is easily adaptable to modern large language model. Its central limitation is performance degradation when irrelevant contexts accompany a query. More accurate question-context relevance measurement, including a relevance estimator, improves open-domain QA performance and interpretability; RE-RAG outperforms traditional RAG with the same total parameters. High-confidence retrieved context enables efficient use by small models, while alternative knowledge sources help in low-confidence cases. Further modules remain a direction for exploration.

l: relevance estimator (RE), RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The relevance estimator (RE) is a detachable relevance-evaluation component in RE-RAG for retrieval-augmented generation and open-domain QA. It measures precise relative relevance between a question or query and retrieved contexts, estimates confidence that a context is useful for answering, and can be weakly supervised from question-answer data without explicit question-context compatibility labels. Using the same question-context input as a generator, it employs a sequence-to-sequence architecture to generate a “true” or “false” classification token. The normalized probability of “true” is converted to a logit, providing relevance scores for reranking and weighted answer marginalization. In use, RE evaluates an initial set of 100 retrieved contexts, reranks them, and selects the top 25 for inference; it also identifies context sets whose top 25 lack an answer through true-token probabilities. Jointly fine-tuned with a small language model, it improves that generator, and after separation it can be applied to large language models. It improves retrieval-augmented generation reliability, supports confidence-aware decoding, and improves large language models when combined with them. Reported results show stronger reranking than the retriever, FiD-KD, and Recall@k comparisons, better unseen-dataset generalization than FiD-KD, and better unanswerable-set classification F1 than MonoT5, with higher precision than the retriever and balanced precision and recall. When applied to Llama2, it surpasses Self-RAG.

l: context, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A context is information retrieved from an external knowledge base and paired with a question for retrieval-augmented QA. It is encoded as an embedding independently of the question and used by the model generator to produce answers. Its relevance is crucial: irrelevant or low-confidence contexts can distract the language model, cause it to parrot misleading material, and reduce answer accuracy. In RE-RAG, a relevance estimator reranks retrieved contexts so top-ranked ones are used for generation. Training uses top 20 contexts, while development and testing provide 100 and inference selects 25. Context sets may be answerable or unanswerable, shaping reranking and whether contextual or parametric knowledge is used.

s: Confidence indicates whether retrieved contexts are useful for answering a question. It is measured by a relevance estimator and guides decoding strategies: use retrieved context when appropriate, classify the query as unanswerable when confidence is low, or selectively rely on an LLM’s parametric knowledge.

l: query, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The query is evaluated against retrieved contexts to judge their relevance and usefulness for answering. A confidence-based decoding strategy measures whether a context truly helps; if the context set is irrelevant or unsupported, the query is classified as unanswerable.

l: weakly supervised method, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A method trains a relevance estimator using question-answer data without labels identifying correct contexts.

l: sLM, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: sLM is a small generator with 2B parameters or fewer and scarce parametric knowledge. It trains a relevance estimator, which improves the sLM when fine-tuned together and can later be separated for large language models.

l: LLM, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Large language models are models with 7B parameters or more and abundant parametric knowledge, including GPT and Llama. They are used in in-context learning and by RALM with concatenated context. A relevance estimator trained on a small language model can help them choose parametric knowledge when retrieved contexts have low confidence or are unreliable. Although FiD methods limit them because they require encoded data, their development renewed attention to RAG models that directly input context. Combined with a detachable relevance estimator, they improve performance.

l: decoding strategies, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The decoding strategies use confidence measured by a relevance estimator to judge whether retrieved context is useful for a query. When the context set is irrelevant or low-confidence, they can first classify the question as unanswerable and tell the user, or instead selectively rely on the language model’s parametric knowledge rather than unrelated contexts. Thus, answering proceeds from relevance-confidence assessment to either an unanswerable response or parametric-knowledge use.

l: knowledge-intensive tasks, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Knowledge-intensive tasks are identified as a specific area in which retrieval augmented generation has shown promising progress.

l: retrieval-augmented language modeling (RALM), RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RALM is an in-context learning approach for large-language models that utilizes concatenated context.

l: document relevance scores, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The relevance distribution is formed by applying a softmax to the relevance-estimator logits across contexts. RE-RAG uses this distribution, PRE(qi,cj), to weight context-specific generator probabilities.

l: in-context learning, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a approach [for large-language models (LLMs)] In-context learning is presented as the approach used by RALM, which provides concatenated context to large-language models.

l: question, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The question is encoded by the retriever, paired with each context, and used to assess similarity and relevance, train relevance estimation without explicit compatibility labels, and support answer generation.

l: RE score, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A relevance metric measures relative context-query relevance; precise scores support aggregated answers through marginalization, while imprecise scores direct attention to documents less likely to answer.

l: unanswerable set classification, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Unanswerable set classification detects retrieved top-25 context sets with no gold answer by treating irrelevant sets as unanswerable. A relevance estimator uses a dev-set F1-selected threshold and outperforms FiD-KD and MonoT5 in F1 on NQ and TQA through a better precision-recall balance. Classifying low-confidence sets this way substantially improves unanswerable-set performance while causing only minor loss on answerable sets; FiD-KD is less effective under this trade-off.

l: retriever, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retriever is a component that searches an external knowledge base and returns related context sets. It commonly uses a bi-encoder and independently generated embeddings to calculate question-context similarity. It is fast and effective, supplying top 20 contexts for training and top 100 for development, testing, and re-ranking, plus top-25 sets for unanswerable classification. There it has higher recall but lower precision and F1 than the relevance estimator.

l: generator, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Generator is a sequence-to-sequence model that takes a question and context and produces an answer with probability. Its answer likelihood supplies a joint-training signal to a separate context-relevance estimator. It uses T5 or Flan-T5 components; experiments report small and large generators separately, including Llama2, Llama3, ChatGPT, and Codex.

l: answer, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: An answer is generated separately for each question-context pair and can then be marginalized across contexts. The training objective uses the ground-truth answer ai and the generator probability for that answer.

l: RAG-sequence, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RAG-sequence marginalizes answer probabilities across individual contexts, achieving higher performance than RAG-token while supporting interpretable answer generation.

l: answer marginalization, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Answer marginalization aggregates context-specific answer probabilities, first weighting them by normalized similarity scores in traditional RAG and later by relevance-estimator scores in RE-RAG.

l: retriever similarity score, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retriever similarity score is computed by dot product of independently encoded question and context embeddings, enabling top-k retrieval and weighting answer marginalization.

l: generator probability distribution, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The generator probability distribution is formed by computing the log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer for each retrieved context and applying a softmax across contexts. QG(qi,cj) represents the relative relevance implied by the generator.

l: Lgen, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: A negative likelihood loss combines ground-truth answer likelihood with relevance-estimator probability, training the generator and relevance classification-token probability together.

l: Lre, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Lre is a KL-divergence loss between PRE and QG, training the relevance estimator without labeled relevance data to improve answer performance.

l: Ltot, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Ltot is a joint training objective combining Lgen with scaled Lre and Ltok; α1 and α2 balance relevance and token losses.

l: joint training, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: uses Ltot [to train the two models jointly] Joint training optimizes the generator and relevance estimator with three losses: Lgen, Lre, and Ltok. Ltok penalizes the relevance estimator for assigning probability to tokens other than "true" and "false."

l: Natural Questions, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Natural Questions is an open-domain QA dataset used for evaluation, built from real web-user questions with long-answer contexts and short-answer spans. Experiments use NQ-open, retaining questions whose short answers contain at most five tokens. Denoted NQ, it is one of two datasets used to evaluate RE-RAG and is more knowledge-intensive than TriviaQA. RE-RAG performs better on NQ; mixed strategy usually avoids major losses, while parametric knowledge helps less, especially for Llama 2 models.

l: TriviaQA, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: TriviaQA is an open-domain question-answer dataset collected from trivia enthusiasts and reviewed by human annotators, used for evaluation in unfiltered form. It is used to evaluate RE-RAG, appears more dependent on generator models than Natural Questions, and benefits from selectively using parametric knowledge for low-confidence context sets; mixed strategies usually improve reported performance.

l: FiD, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: FiD is a retrieval-augmented generation question-answering system with powerful open-domain QA performance, outperforming RAG-based systems. FiDbase and FiDlarge use 100 contexts for inference; later models leveraged its structural advantages, while large language models face limitations from methods requiring encoded data.

l: FiD-KD, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: FiD-KD is a retriever and baseline used with large language models, including for zero-shot RALM, reranking, and unanswerable-set classification. It retrieves top-100 contexts, uses knowledge distillation through FiD attention scores, and its base and large variants are evaluated with 25 or 100 contexts. It reaches R@1 recall of 49.4 on Natural Questions and 60.1 on TriviaQA. Its scores support reranking better than traditional RAG answer generation, but RE outperforms it on reranking recall and F1; FiD-KD degrades more on unseen datasets and loses answerable-set accuracy under low-confidence classification.

l: Llama 3, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Llama 3 is a set of models evaluated with retrieval-augmented and parametric decoding; on TriviaQA, model sizes converge at high confidence but diverge more at low confidence.

l: exact match, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Exact match is the primary evaluation metric: normalized generated answers are correct only when they exactly match one of the dataset's correct answers.

l: T5, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: T5 is a generative model used by the relevance estimator and generator, identified in open-domain QA research.

l: question-answering performance, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Question-answering performance focuses on single-hop QA, evaluating complete RAG on Natural Questions and TriviaQA; RE-RAG improves over traditional RAG and competes with FiD, while TriviaQA depends more on the generator.

l: re-ranking, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_evaluated_with retrieval accuracy [using Recall@k] The relevance estimator is evaluated as a re-ranker over the top-100 contexts retrieved by FiD-KD. It achieves higher Recall@1, Recall@5, Recall@10, and Recall@20 than FiD-KD and MonoT5 on both NQ and TQA, with greater efficiency when fewer contexts are used.

l: low-confidence context set, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Low-confidence context sets, identified by relevance-estimator confidence, drive classification strategy: small language models may answer unanswerably, while large models may switch to parametric knowledge; the RE module supplies relevance and confidence for decoding decisions.

l: confidence score, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_determined_by maximum value of the “true” token probability [for contexts within the set] The confidence score is determined by the maximum probability assigned to the “true” token by the relevance estimator for contexts in a set. Thresholds selected for classification performance determine when the model should answer “unanswerable” or use parametric knowledge.

l: mixed strategy, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: The mixed strategy uses retrieved context at high confidence and otherwise bypasses it for the largest model’s parametric knowledge, producing mainly TriviaQA gains that are larger for smaller models when parametric knowledge is effective.

l: Question Answering, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: performance_improves_with external knowledge [according to previous research] Question Answering systems can improve their performance by utilizing external knowledge about questions. Research has also studied more accurate retrieval of external knowledge to make these systems more efficient.

l: BART, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a generative models BART is identified as a generative model used in open-domain QA research.

l: traditional RAG, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Traditional RAG achieves powerful open-domain QA performance, improves with a BERT-based reranker requiring additional high-quality labels, and is extended by RE-RAG with improved performance.

l: Atlas, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: achieves state-of-the-art performance [through an improved retriever and scaling up the model] Atlas achieved state-of-the-art performance through an improved retriever and scaling up the model.

l: GPT, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: GPT is identified as a large language model developed in recent years.

l: Llama, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Llama is identified as a large language model developed in recent years.

l: RAG models, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RAG models receive renewed attention because large language models can directly input context; approaches improve performance by training retrievers applicable to large language models or by reviewing questions and context within the model.

l: single-hop QA tasks, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a QA tasks [single-hop] The research has primarily focused on improving answer performance in single-hop QA tasks.

l: multi-hop QA tasks, RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a QA tasks [multi-hop] The effectiveness of the proposed framework has not been sufficiently verified in multi-hop QA tasks. Future research may explore extending the RE-RAG framework to these tasks.

s: cannot_be_adequately_answered_using parametric knowledge [truly unanswerable] A truly unanswerable query is defined as one that cannot be adequately answered even when the model's parametric knowledge is used. The text states that further research is needed to detect this condition accurately.

l: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: The paper introduces personalized large-language-model agents for smartphone AI assistants, using users’ personal memories to improve question answering, autofill forms, and user services, with related uses such as reminders and travel navigation. Its central problem is how to collect practical memory data, let users’ changing memories be edited, and selectively retrieve and combine the relevant memories for each task. The proposed framework, EMG-RAG, combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation with an Editable Memory Graph (EMG) and reinforcement learning. Memory data are gathered from conversations and screenshots; GPT-4 is used for memory and question-answer-pair generation. The EMG organizes hierarchical memory types and entity relationships, while an RL agent treats graph traversal and memory choice as an MDP, selecting memories for a frozen base language model to use in answering requests. The framework also supports dynamic edits and online learning to mitigate cold start. The work situates itself alongside personalized dialogue, knowledge-graph RAG, and model-editing research, including PersonaChat and P2BOT, but focuses on practical memories collected by smartphone AI assistants and on deployment into an AI assistant product. Experiments use a real-world business dataset with about 11.35 billion raw text items and 0.35 billion memories. Across GPT-4, ChatGLM3-6B, and PanGu-38B, EMG-RAG consistently surpasses RAG baselines on the three applications and on continuous edits; GPT-4 generally produces the strongest results. The paper reports roughly a 10% improvement over the best existing approach, supported by ablation, parameter, online A/B, and data-quality studies, and reports improved usability after transfer to a real smartphone assistant. A limitation is that only the RL agent is trained while LLMs stay fixed. Training is no more efficient than Naive RAG because optimization requires querying the LLM for answers.

l: user data, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Memories are continuously generated on personal devices, then managed and utilized to deliver services to users.

l: memories, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Memories are key, cleaned information units extracted from raw user data, including smartphone conversations, screenshots, emails, calendars, location histories, travel activities, and other apps. They are organized chronologically in an Editable Memory Graph, where they can be inserted, deleted, replaced, and selectively retrieved as they evolve. Personalized agents select relevant memories, sometimes combine multiple memories through a base language model, and use them to ground question answering and enhance downstream applications. Selecting essential memories and modeling their complex relationships improves performance.

l: users, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Users interact with personalized agents through smartphone AI assistant platforms. Their dynamic memory data can cause agent responses to be inserted, deleted, or replaced.

l: personalized agents, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Personalized agents are LLM-powered agents for smartphone AI assistant platforms. Constructed from practical memory data gathered from assistants, including conversations, screenshots, memories, and question-answer pairs, they use and retrieve users’ personal memories to help perform personalized tasks. Their essential capabilities include selecting relevant memories, editability, and selectability in practical use. They support and enhance downstream applications such as question answering, autofill forms, user services, reminders, and travel navigation. The agents are transferred into a real smartphone AI assistant, where they improve usability and user experience by answering questions and providing personalized services.

l: large language models, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Large language models power personalized agents that use smartphone memories to improve downstream applications. They provide semantic understanding and reasoning for personal AI assistants, receiving questions with selected user memories and generating answers. Rather than relying on global knowledge, frozen models use retrieval-augmented generation to respond to changes in the EMG. Their fixed parameters remain unchanged during training, while answer quality evaluates and rewards memory selection.

l: three downstream applications, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: The three downstream applications are enhanced by personalized agents that leverage users' personal memories.

l: EMG-RAG, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: EMG-RAG is a solution and RAG method for personalized agents that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation with an Editable Memory Graph (EMG) and is optimized with Reinforcement Learning. It addresses data collection, editability, and selectability challenges. EMG-RAG first constructs and edits personalized memory graphs, using EMG to capture complex relationships between memories. It then selects essential and activated memories, retrieves relevant memories, and uses them for large language model generation. Training uses warm-start and policy gradient; its implementation uses Python 3.7, Faiss for index construction, TransE for entity and relation embeddings, and CPT-Text for question and memory embeddings. It supports question answering, autofill forms, reminders, travel-related user services, and continuous edits. Evaluations report performance approximately 10% above the best existing approach and outperform M-RAG; for GPT-4 question answering, it achieves 88.06 ROUGE-L and 75.99 BLEU.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a technique and retrieval-augmented generation method that selects relevant memories for a question and provides them as context to a large language model. It is used in EMG-RAG with an Editable Memory Graph for smartphone memories and personalized agents. It retrieves top-K memories, activates graph nodes, and uses an MDP to traverse the edited graph before generation. Its key concerns are context overhead, noise, and missed diverse memory combinations; it is evaluated through indexing, retrieval, and generation.

l: Editable Memory Graph, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Editable Memory Graph is a three-layer data structure and multilayered structure for managing users’ personal memories, with the user as the root node. Its Memory Type Layer and Memory Subclass Layer form a tree organized by business scopes, and its memory graph is entity-based, capturing complex relationships among memories. It supports insertion, deletion, replacement, and dynamic user edits, as well as efficient retrieval and selection of essential memories within relevant partitions. Combined with Retrieval-Augmented Generation and a frozen large language model in EMG-RAG, it addresses data collection, editability, and selectability; removing activated nodes reduces question-answering performance.

l: Reinforcement Learning, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Reinforcement Learning further optimizes EMG-RAG, addressing data collection, editability, and selectability. It models retrieval-augmented generation by optimizing graph memory selection end to end. Selected memories prompt a frozen large language model; improved answer quality supplies rewards. Training starts with supervised warm-starting, then uses REINFORCE policy gradients, with ROUGE and BLEU as example evaluation metrics.

l: data collection, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Data collection gathers conversations and screenshots, uses OCR to extract content, generates memories and question-answer pairs, and uses GPT-4 for training labels.

l: editability, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Editability allows responses from personalized agents to be changed based on users’ dynamic memory data. The changes can involve insertion, deletion, and replacement operations.

l: selectability, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Selectability enables personalized agents to select memories relevant to users’ queries. Some queries require multiple memories to be combined through a base language model to generate responses.

l: smartphone AI assistant, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: A smartphone AI assistant is a platform and setting for user-personalized agents, supplying practical memory from conversations, screenshots, and interactions. After receiving transferred personalized agents, it gains enhanced usability; Siri and Bixby are mentioned as examples.

l: RL agent, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: The RL agent, the trained component, adaptively selects Editable Memory Graph memories without fixed Top-K limits, improving answer quality generated by a frozen large language model.

l: GPT-4, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: GPT-4 is an OpenAI-developed, Transformer-based pre-trained large language model known for human-level performance. It cleans raw business data into tagged personal memories, generates session question-answer pairs, and produces ground-truth answers and key entities for self-verifying data quality. With EMG-RAG it yields the strongest reported downstream results, though its questions differ from real users' in online A/B evaluation.

l: real-world business dataset, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: A real-world business dataset collected from an AI assistant product, containing daily assistant-user conversations and app screenshots from March through June 2024. Its roughly 11.35 billion raw text items are cleaned into about 0.35 billion memories, used to extract personal memories, evaluate personalized agents, and sample 2,000 training and 500 testing users.

l: question answering, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Question answering is a downstream EMG-RAG application for smartphone AI assistants, using relevant memories to generate user answers. It is evaluated against GPT-4-generated ground truth with ROUGE and BLEU; GPT-4 with EMG-RAG reports strong scores and improves performance by about 10.6% over the best existing approach.

l: autofill forms, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Autofill forms is a downstream application for evaluating personalized agents. It uses a user’s memories to generate key entities, such as a mobile number, for completing online flight and hotel booking forms. Evaluated by Exact Match accuracy, GPT-4 with EMG-RAG reaches 92.86%, outperforming M-RAG by 2.2 points.

l: user services, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: User services are a downstream application evaluated on a real-world business dataset. They provide reminders of recent or important events and times and travel assistance with destination addresses for navigation, with information usable in calendar or map applications. EMG-RAG improves performance, reaching 96.43% for reminders and 91.46% for travel.

l: personalized dialogue system, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: A personalized dialogue system is developed using persona and chat data, with research addressing mutual persona perception, persona sparsity, and long-term persona memory. It can also be enhanced through internal reasoning or external acting techniques.

l: PersonaChat, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: PersonaChat is a crowdsourced dataset of profile-defined personas and chats between paired workers, supporting personalized dialogue systems.

l: P2BOT, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: uses GPT P2BOT is a GPT-based framework designed to enrich personalized dialogue generation through mutual persona perception. It models underlying understanding, such as character traits, to facilitate mutual acquaintance between interlocutors.

l: retrieval-augmented generation on knowledge graph, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: is_a RAG approach [reviewed across various tasks] Retrieval-augmented generation on knowledge graphs has been studied across KBQA, open-domain scenarios, table-related tasks, human-machine conversation, and image captioning. In this study, it is used with a frozen large language model to respond to dynamic changes in personal memories.

l: knowledge graph, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Knowledge graphs are used as the basis for retrieval-augmented generation across several tasks. The study uses a graph-based memory structure and optimizes memory selection on the graph.

l: model editing, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: edits pre-trained language model [within specific domains while preserving performance across other domains] Model editing is described as research focused on correcting model predictions as real-world information changes while preserving performance in other domains. Existing approaches include learnable editors, activation adjustments for stored facts, and external memories that retrieve relevant edits.

l: continuous edits, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Continuous edits dynamically modify EMG, are incorporated by M-RAG, and over four weeks EMG-RAG supports them while outperforming M-RAG across question answering, autofill forms, and user services.

l: dynamic memory data, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Dynamic memory data belongs to users, modifies agent responses, and supports insertion, deletion, and replacement across usage scenarios.

l: question-answer pair, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: is_a training data [for personalized agents using EMG-RAG] Question-answer pairs are generated from several memories and include the memories required to answer each question. They are used to train the memory-selection process and the personalized agent.

l: Editable Memory Graph construction, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
s: Editable Memory Graph construction uses four predefined memory types, Relationship, Preference, Event, and Attribute, and subclass partitions. Entity recognition creates nodes, relation extraction creates edges, and TransE embeddings connect entities with nearby subclasses.

l: memory graph, Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs

l: Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: This preliminary study, "Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation," tests whether Generative Pre-trained Transformers, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, can automatically assess human tutors’ social-emotional tutoring practices and support personalized tutor training. It analyzes five transcripts from real-world United States Zoom math tutoring sessions for Grades 6–8, led by novice tutors who circulated among students in breakout rooms. The evaluations use a rubric built around five social-emotional learning and relationship-building principles, including process-focused praise, growth-mindset encouragement, helping students correct errors, responding to negative self-talk, building self-efficacy, and motivational strategies. The researchers compare four prompting approaches: two Basic Zero-shot prompt types, Tree of Thoughts, and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) prompt. These approaches generate tutoring-practice scores and evidence-based interpretations, using either binary or 0–5 scoring criteria. In the RAG approach, tutoring transcripts and social-emotional learning principles are converted to word embeddings, selectively retrieved, and used to generate scores and evidence. A human coder judges generated assessments for correctness and hallucination, while the study tracks GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4 Turbo token costs. Results show GPT-3.5 generally performs poorly, whereas RAG produces correct, non-hallucinated evaluations; GPT-4 is more accurate overall, with RAG and Zero-shot P1 performing best. RAG consistently delivers the desired output across both models, is the most cost-effective strategy, and provides accurate, contextually relevant assessments. GPT-4 Turbo costs about ten times as much as GPT-3.5 Turbo. The study plans to expand to more competencies and transcripts and develop a training-lesson recommender system.

l: novice human tutors, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Novice human tutors teach Grade 6–8 math in one-on-one sessions while managing and circulating among three to five breakout rooms, leaving students when they seem able to work independently. Before tutoring, they complete social-emotional learning lessons through a tutor training platform, yet often prioritize content-specific guidance and neglect social-emotional learning during tutoring.

l: social-emotional learning, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Social-emotional learning is a set of competencies including self-awareness, empathy, relationship-building, and critical decision-making. It is crucial for students’ holistic development, nurturing tutor-student relationships, equity, and inclusion; neglect during tutoring is associated with reduced effectiveness. In this study, it begins in lessons completed by human tutors before sessions, then informs principles and rubrics for assessing tutoring transcripts. Those principles are converted into word embeddings for a RAG-based prompt, making social-emotional learning the basis of tutoring-quality evaluations, with planned extension to other competencies.

l: Generative Pre-trained Transformers, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Generative Pre-trained Transformers are large language models, including GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, investigated for automatically assessing human tutors’ social-emotional competencies. Using RAG-based prompts, they selectively retrieve database information and analyze tutoring transcripts according to specified principles and rubrics. They generate assessment scores, evidence, interpretations, and feedback, supporting evaluation of accuracy and financial feasibility for real-time, large-scale use. Across prompt strategies, GPT-4 generally yields more accurate evaluations than GPT-3.5, while RAG-based prompting performs consistently well across versions.

l: GPT-3.5 Turbo, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: GPT-3.5 Turbo is a Generative Pre-trained Transformer evaluated for assessing tutors’ social-emotional tutoring competencies, with performance and cost compared with GPT-4. Its financial cost was calculated from prompt, transcript, and generated-text tokens. Under prompting strategies other than Retrieval-Augmented Generation, it generally failed to provide the desired evaluation and hallucinated negative self-talk absent from the transcript. Its RAG-based strategy cost $0.008 per lesson evaluation, the lowest listed and about one-tenth of GPT-4 Turbo’s cost.

l: GPT-4 Turbo, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: GPT-4 Turbo, a Generative Pre-trained Transformer, is evaluated for assessing tutors’ social-emotional tutoring competencies against GPT-3.5. Its financial cost is calculated from prompt, transcript, and generated-text tokens across prompts. Results show generally more accurate evaluations, especially with RAG and Zero-shot (P1). In conclusion, it costs about 10 times more per lesson than GPT-3.5 Turbo; RAG costs $0.137 and provides accurate evaluations without hallucinations.

l: assessment of tutoring practices, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Assessment of tutoring practices evaluates tutors’ social-emotional learning competencies from tutoring transcripts using five categories: Giving Effective Praise, Supporting a Growth Mindset, Reacting to Errors, Responding to Negative Self-Talk, and Using Motivational Strategies. Based on research-based social-emotional learning and relationship-building principles, it aims to reduce routine reliance on scarce human experts. The study prompts GPT models to generate scores and interpretations, compares multiple prompting strategies, and concludes that Retrieval-Augmented Generation performs accurately while costing less than the other evaluated prompts.

l: personalized tutor training, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Assessment of tutors’ social-emotional competencies guides personalized tutor training, informing interventions that subsequently improve tutoring’s educational effectiveness.

l: Prompting Strategies, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Prompting Strategies are four prompt types designed for GPT models to evaluate tutor performance and tutoring practices through criteria, scores, and evidence-based interpretation. They comprise Basic Zero-shot Prompt Types I and II, Tree of Thought Prompt, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation Based Prompt. The study begins by defining and designing these strategies, then assesses them for hallucination, correctness, cost, and evaluation accuracy. Results compare their effects: Retrieval-Augmented Generation performs consistently well, while GPT-4’s Zero-shot Prompt Type I is more accurate than other strategies. The conclusion identifies Retrieval-Augmented Generation as the most cost-effective strategy for both GPT models while supporting accurate evaluations.

l: Zero-shot prompting, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Two basic Zero-shot prompt strategies are evaluated for automatically assessing tutors’ social-emotional tutoring strategies. They are compared with Tree of Thought and Retrieval-Augmented Generator-based prompting.

l: Tree of Thoughts, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Tree of Thoughts is a prompt strategy structured as branches of a tree, reported by Yao et al. (2023), for GPT-based assessment of tutors’ social-emotional competencies. It organizes tutoring-transcript information and evaluates a tutor in a competency area using Social Emotional Learning Principles and criteria. Across three layers, it scores performance, identifies met and unmet criteria, and produces a numbered rubric-based evaluation with supporting evidence, scores, and interpretations. It is examined alongside Zero-shot and Retrieval-Augmented Generator-based prompts.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a RAG-based prompt strategy and prompt-based evaluation approach that integrates external knowledge sources into prompting. For tutoring practice evaluation, it uses word embeddings to bring tutoring transcripts and tutoring principles into a GPT model, allowing prepared embeddings to supply relevant information, including social-emotional learning principles, for scores and evidence. Its Retriever identifies correct and incorrect uses of a practice and returns tutor dialogue as evidence; its Generator produces a final 0-to-5 score, with one point for each criterion met. Across GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, the strategy consistently produces the desired output. It yields correct, contextually relevant, precise evaluations of tutoring transcripts without hallucinations, with accuracy assessed through hallucination levels and correctness in generated assessment texts. It demonstrates more accurate performance and lower financial costs than the other evaluated prompting strategies, and is identified as the most cost-effective strategy for GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4 Turbo. It is proposed for broader tutor assessment applications, including a wider range of real-world tutoring transcripts and assessment of building content skills and promoting inclusion.

l: Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: This is a paper in the Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, titled “Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs.” Simone Conia, Daniel Lee, Min Li, Umar Farooq Minhas, Saloni Potdar, and Yunyao Li present work from Sapienza University of Rome, Adobe, and Apple on translating text whose entity names, such as movies, books, foods, locations, and sometimes people, have culturally variable target-language forms. The paper argues that advances in multilingual models and data have not resolved this entity-name problem. It introduces XC-Translate, a manually curated benchmark of over 58,000 instances and more than 100,000 human-produced references across 10 English-to-X language pairs. Built from short English knowledge-seeking questions, its translations were created and verified by qualified annotators. The authors also introduce M-ETA, a manually based metric for checking whether valid target-language entity names occur in a translation. To address the task, the paper proposes KG-MT, an end-to-end retrieval-augmented translation method using multilingual knowledge graphs, with Wikidata as its reference source. A retriever identifies relevant entities, and a knowledge-enhanced translator uses their source- and target-language names. Explicit integration provides entity translations in the input, while implicit integration combines entity embeddings with encoder representations; the two approaches are complementary. Experiments compare GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, multilingual MT systems, and KG-MT on XC-Translate and WMT benchmarks. Existing systems, including NLLB-200 and GPT-4, perform relatively well on conventional metrics but struggle on entity-aware M-ETA evaluation. KG-MTNLLB achieves the best average M-ETA, and KG-MT is reported to improve over NLLB-200 and GPT-4 by 129% and 62% relatively. Its WMT BLEU and COMET results remain competitive or slightly improved, suggesting no loss of general translation quality. Retrieval reaches 85.9% hits@1 and 92.1% hits@3, although the translator does not always use even gold knowledge effectively. The paper concludes that retrieval-augmented translation can improve cross-cultural entity translation and may extend to idioms and metaphors. It notes limitations in language and entity coverage, Wikidata-related bias, incomplete evaluation metrics, retrieval capped at three entities, and comparison-system coverage. The work was carried out mainly while Conia and Lee were at Apple.

s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a method for cross-cultural machine translation: KG-MT retrieves from multilingual knowledge graphs, using low-frequency words at inference or fuzzy training matches to improve translation.

l: Multilingual Knowledge Graphs, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: Multilingual Knowledge Graphs provide lexical and factual information about millions of entities in many languages, including names, aliases, and descriptions. Easier to edit and frequently updated for real-world changes, they serve as KG-MT’s retrieval source for retrieval-augmented generation. KG-MT retrieves and integrates their information to improve entity-aware translation, especially for texts containing entity names, across backbones and language pairs.

l: cross-cultural translation, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: Cross-cultural translation is a problem centered on translating texts containing entity names whose culturally specific references can differ across languages, sometimes requiring changes beyond transliteration or through transcreation. It matters because the area lacks large-scale, high-quality benchmarks that expose these challenges. The work addresses the problem through resources and methods: it introduces XC-Translate, a benchmark for short, relatively simple surrounding texts with entity-name differences, and KG-MT, a system intended to capture cross-language and cross-cultural differences. It concludes that challenges vary by language and that broader language coverage is needed for robust, generalizable systems.

l: entity names in machine translation, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: Entity names are culturally nuanced translation content whose forms can vary greatly across languages, making text that contains them difficult for machine translation systems and large language models. The discussion begins with their cultural importance, then explains that movies, books, food, locations, and sometimes people may need contextually appropriate rather than literal translations. It concludes that prior work has emphasized transliteration, while transcreation, large-scale benchmarks, and methods without synthetic augmentation or frequent retraining need more study.

l: XC-Translate, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: XC-Translate is a large-scale, manually created and verified machine-translation evaluation benchmark for cross-cultural translation of text containing potentially culturally nuanced entity names. It covers 10 English-to-X language pairs, with Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, Thai, and Turkish as target languages. It contains about 5,000 sentences per language pair, more than 58,000 instances, and over 100,000 references, averaging two translations per sentence. Human annotators selected entity names likely to require treatment beyond transliteration. The benchmark is designed to reveal weaknesses in MT systems and multilingual large language models when entity names vary culturally. Evaluation results show that BLEU and COMET can remain high despite incorrect entity translations, while M-ETA reports substantially lower entity-aware performance. It also evaluates a knowledge retriever, which reaches 85.9% hits@1 and 92.1% hits@3; KG-MT significantly outperforms the state of the art. Although diverse, XC-Translate is not exhaustive: it omits Uralic, Dravidian, and Niger-Congo families, many Indo-European languages, and dialectal and regional variation; its Wikidata-based entity selection may also exclude culturally relevant entities.

l: machine translation, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: Cross-cultural translation of texts containing culturally nuanced entity names is a research topic in natural language processing. Although machine translation has advanced through multilingual language models, large multilingual datasets, and systems such as mBART-50, M2M-100, and NLLB-200, current systems still struggle with this setting, especially potentially for low-resource languages and dialects. XC-Translate is introduced as a benchmark for the task. Its English questions are translated into target languages by at least three human translators per question, then verified by at least three separate human annotators per translation. Evaluations compare machine translation systems and LLMs with KG-MT; KG-MT outperforms NLLB-200 and GPT-4 on XC-Translate while generally preserving or slightly improving quality on general-purpose WMT benchmarks.

l: KG-MT, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: KG-MT is a novel end-to-end, knowledge-graph-based machine translation system and retrieval-augmented translation approach. It improves translation of texts containing entity names by using dense retrieval to obtain relevant entity names from a multilingual knowledge graph on the fly at inference time, rather than requiring memorization of every entity-name translation through synthetic data augmentation. KG-MT unfolds through two main components: a knowledge retriever, which retrieves knowledge, and a knowledge-enhanced translator, which translates with that knowledge. Retrieved information is integrated explicitly by adding entity names to the source text, implicitly by fusing entity embeddings with encoder hidden states, or through both methods; the components' representations are also fused to enable closer interaction. The two integration methods are complementary, and their combination gives the best results. Across MT backbones and language pairs, KG-MT and its variants substantially outperform baselines on XC-Translate in M-ETA, including reported relative improvements of 129% over NLLB-200 and 62% over GPT-4. It requires minimal supervision and computational resources compared with data augmentation approaches, while maintaining competitive or comparable general-purpose translation quality on WMT and other general-purpose MT benchmarks. With gold entities, average M-ETA improves by 11.6%, showing that the knowledge-enhanced translator does not always use gold knowledge effectively.

l: knowledge retriever, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: The knowledge retriever is a dense retrieval mechanism for KG-MT that collects the most relevant knowledge-graph entities for a source text. It represents entities with primary names and descriptions, defines relevance with cosine similarity, and contrastively trains an encoder on Mintaka. Its fine-tuning uses hard negative mining, including homonymous entities sharing a relevant entity’s name. For each source text, it returns the top relevant entities but at most three, balancing relevance against computational cost. On XC-Translate, it reaches 85.9% hits@1 and 92.1% hits@3; hard negative mining improves these by 5.6% and 4.2% versus mContriever. Whether the three-entity limit suits longer documents is unclear.

l: large language models, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: Large language models are examined in experiments showing persistent difficulty translating texts with entity names, especially across cultures; the study focuses mainly on the GPT family and suggests future examination of openly available models.

l: NLLB-200, Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
s: NLLB-200 is a multilingual machine-translation model and backbone supporting translation involving about 200 languages through one model. It records the highest average M-ETA among listed MT baselines, 17.9%, plus 23.3 BLEU and 60.2 COMET on EN-to-XX WMT-17–21 tests. It is used as a comparison baseline, which KG-MT variants surpass.
